questions.question:
If ‘\( \rightarrow \)’ denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [drizzle \( \rightarrow \) rain \( \rightarrow \) downpour] is analogous to [______ \( \rightarrow \) quarrel \( \rightarrow \) feud].
Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
questions.explanation:
Verbal Aptitude → Vocabulary

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Core Concept(s): Semantic intensity and word analogy.
  • Given: A progression of words related to precipitation based on increasing intensity.
  • Find: A corresponding word to complete a similar progression of increasing intensity for the word "quarrel".

Solution

  • The relationship defined is "increasing order of intensity" (drizzle → rain → downpour).
  • We must identify a word that represents a milder, lower-intensity form of a quarrel.
  • A feud is an extended and bitter quarrel, representing the highest intensity in the given sequence.
  • To bicker means to argue about petty or trivial matters, which logically serves as the lower-intensity precursor.
  • The words bog, dither, and dodge do not relate to arguments or conflicts.
  • The complete logical progression is: bicker → quarrel → feud.

Answer: (A) bicker

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | GA Q2
questions.subject: General Aptitude
questions.question:
Statements:
1. All heroes are winners.
2. All winners are lucky people.
Inferences:
I. All lucky people are heroes.
II. Some lucky people are heroes.
III. Some winners are heroes.
Which of the above inferences can be logically deduced from statements 1 and 2?
questions.explanation:
Analytical Aptitude → Logic

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): Syllogistic reasoning, Venn Diagrams.
  • Given: Two universal affirmative statements: All heroes are winners; All winners are lucky people.
  • Find: Which of the three provided inferences logically follow from the statements.

Solution

  • Let \(H\), \(W\), and \(L\) denote the sets of heroes, winners, and lucky people, respectively.
  • The given statements define strict subset relations: \(H \subseteq W\) and \(W \subseteq L\). By transitivity, it is guaranteed that \(H \subseteq L\).
  • Inference I (All lucky people are heroes): Translates to \(L \subseteq H\). This is invalid; the converse of a universal affirmative is not necessarily true.
  • Inference II (Some lucky people are heroes): Translates to \(L \cap H \neq \emptyset\). Since \(H \subseteq L\) and the set of heroes \(H\) is implicitly non-empty, their intersection exists. This is valid. ✓
  • Inference III (Some winners are heroes): Translates to \(W \cap H \neq \emptyset\). Since \(H \subseteq W\), the intersection is similarly non-empty. This is valid. ✓

Final Answer

Answer: (B) Only II and III

questions.question: A student was supposed to multiply a positive real number \( p \) with another positive real number \( q \). Instead, the student divided \( p \) by \( q \). If the percentage error in the student’s answer is 80%, the value of \( q \) is
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Computation and Estimation

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Percentage Error Modeling.
  • Given: The true mathematical operation is \(p \cdot q\). The erroneous operation performed is \(\dfrac{p}{q}\). The resultant percentage error is 80%, where \(p, q > 0\).
  • Find: The exact numerical value of \(q\).

Solution

  • The absolute percentage error formula is: \[\text{Error} = \dfrac{|\text{True Value} - \text{Measured Value}|}{\text{True Value}}\]
  • Substituting the given variables: \[0.80 = \dfrac{\left|pq - \dfrac{p}{q}\right|}{pq}\]
  • Since \(p > 0\), divide it out from numerator and denominator: \[0.80 = \left|1 - \dfrac{1}{q^2}\right|\]
  • Case 1: \(1 - \dfrac{1}{q^2} = 0.8 \implies \dfrac{1}{q^2} = 0.2 = \dfrac{1}{5} \implies q^2 = 5 \implies q = \sqrt{5}\)
  • Case 2: \(\dfrac{1}{q^2} - 1 = 0.8 \implies \dfrac{1}{q^2} = 1.8 = \dfrac{9}{5} \implies q^2 = \dfrac{5}{9} \implies q = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\)
  • Comparing against the provided options, only \(q = \sqrt{5}\) is listed.

Final Answer

Answer: (D) \(\sqrt{5}\)

questions.question: The ratio of the number of girls to boys in class VIII is the same as the ratio of the number of boys to girls in class IX. The total number of students (boys and girls) in classes VIII and IX is 450 and 360, respectively. If the number of girls in classes VIII and IX is the same, then the number of girls in each class is
questions.explanation:
Quantitative Aptitude → Numerical Relations and Reasoning

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Core Concept(s): Ratio and Proportion, Quadratic Equations.
  • Given: The ratio of girls to boys in class VIII is identical to the ratio of boys to girls in class IX. Total students: 450 in class VIII and 360 in class IX. The absolute number of girls is the same in both classes.
  • Find: The exact number of girls present in each class.

Solution

  • Let the number of girls in both classes be \(g\).
    Boys in class VIII \(= 450 - g\)
    Boys in class IX \(= 360 - g\)
  • Formulate the equality of ratios: \[\dfrac{g}{450 - g} = \dfrac{360 - g}{g}\]
  • Cross-multiplying: \[g^2 = (450 - g)(360 - g)\]
  • Expanding the right-hand side: \[g^2 = 162000 - 450g - 360g + g^2\]
  • Canceling \(g^2\) from both sides: \[0 = 162000 - 810g\]
  • Solving for \(g\): \[810g = 162000 \implies g = \dfrac{162000}{810} = 200\]

Final Answer

Answer: (B) 200

questions.question:
Seven identical cylindrical chalk-sticks are fitted tightly in a cylindrical container. The figure below shows the arrangement of the chalk-sticks inside the cylinder.



The length of the container is equal to the length of the chalk-sticks. The ratio of the occupied space to the empty space of the container is
questions.explanation:

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Core Concept(s): 2D Circle Packing, Area ratios.
  • Given: Seven identical cylindrical chalks are tightly fitted into a larger cylindrical container of the exact same length.
  • Find: The ratio of the volume of occupied space to the volume of empty space within the container.

Solution

  • Because the lengths of the chalks and the container are identical, the volume ratio reduces to the cross-sectional area ratio.
  • The tightest packing of 7 identical circles within a larger circle: 1 central circle surrounded symmetrically by 6 tangent circles.
  • Let the radius of a small chalk be \(r\). The container's radius spans 3 small circles: \(R = 3r\).
  • Total area occupied by 7 chalk bases: \(7\pi r^2\)
  • Total area of the outer container's base: \(\pi R^2 = \pi(3r)^2 = 9\pi r^2\)
  • Empty space area: \(9\pi r^2 - 7\pi r^2 = 2\pi r^2\)
  • Required ratio: \[\dfrac{\text{Occupied Area}}{\text{Empty Area}} = \dfrac{7\pi r^2}{2\pi r^2} = \dfrac{7}{2}\]

Final Answer

Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{7}{2}\)

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q11
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
A partial differential equation

\[\dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial y^2} = 0 \]

is defined for the two-dimensional field \( T: T(x, y) \), inside a planar square domain of size 2 m × 2 m. Three boundary edges of the square domain are maintained at value \( T = 50 \), whereas the fourth boundary edge is maintained at \( T = 100 \).

The value of \( T \) at the center of the domain is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Partial Differential Equations (Laplace Equation – Dirichlet Problem)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Square domain of size \(2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}\); governing PDE \(\dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial y^2} = 0\); three boundary edges at \(T = 50\); fourth boundary edge at \(T = 100\).
  • Aim: Evaluate \(T\) at the geometric centre of the domain.

Core Concepts:

Laplace's equation \(\nabla^2 T = 0\) admits harmonic solutions. The mean-value property of harmonic functions combined with linearity and the uniqueness theorem for the Dirichlet problem on a square imply that the centre value is exactly the arithmetic average of the four constant boundary temperatures — each side contributes equally by symmetry.

Superposition principle: \(T = 50 + u\), where \(u = 0\) on three sides and \(u = 50\) on the fourth. At the centre, \(u_c = 50/4 = 12.5\), hence \(T_c = 62.5\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. List boundary temperatures: 50, 50, 50, 100.
  2. Each side contributes \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) of its value at the centre (by symmetry).
    \[T_{\text{center}} = \dfrac{50 + 50 + 50 + 100}{4} = \dfrac{250}{4} = 62.5 \]
  3. Verify via superposition:
    \[T = 50 + u \implies u_{\text{center}} = \dfrac{50}{4} = 12.5 \implies T_{\text{center}} = 50 + 12.5 = 62.5 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 62.5 | Correct option: (B)

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra (Matrix Transpose Properties)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Given Data: Matrices \(A\) and \(B\) are conformable for addition and multiplication.
    Statement P: \((A + B)^T = A^T + B^T\)
    Statement Q: \((AB)^T = A^T B^T\)
  • Aim: Identify which statement(s) is/are TRUE.

Core Concepts:

Standard transpose theorems: the sum rule \((A+B)^T = A^T + B^T\) always holds, while the product rule reverses order: \((AB)^T = B^T A^T\) (not \(A^T B^T\) as stated in Q).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. For P — element-wise verification:
    \[ [(A+B)^T]_{ij} = (A+B)_{ji} = A_{ji} + B_{ji} = (A^T)_{ij} + (B^T)_{ij} \]
    \(\therefore\) P is TRUE.
  2. For Q — element-wise verification:
    \[ [(AB)^T]_{ki} = (AB)_{ik} = \sum_j A_{ij} B_{jk} \]
    RHS of Q: \((A^T B^T)_{ki} = \sum_j A_{jk} B_{ij}\) — this does not equal the LHS.
    Correct identity: \((AB)^T = B^T A^T\)
    \(\therefore\) Q is FALSE.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: P is TRUE and Q is FALSE | Correct option: (A)

questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
The second derivative of a function \( f \) is computed using the fourth-order Central Divided Difference method with a step length \( h \).

The CORRECT expression for the second derivative is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Numerical Methods | Finite-Difference Approximations

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Fourth-order central divided-difference scheme with uniform step length \(h\); function values \(f_{i+2},\, f_{i+1},\, f_i,\, f_{i-1},\, f_{i-2}\).
  • Aim: Identify the correct expression for the second derivative \(f''(x_i)\).

Core Concepts:

Taylor series expansion about \(x_i\) up to \(O(h^5)\) terms, followed by algebraic elimination of odd-powered terms, yields the fourth-order accurate central formula for \(f''\). Truncation error is \(O(h^4)\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Taylor Expansions:
    \[f_{i\pm1} = f_i \pm h f'_i + \dfrac{h^2}{2}f''_i \pm \dfrac{h^3}{6}f'''_i + \dfrac{h^4}{24}f^{(4)}_i + O(h^5) \]\[f_{i\pm2} = f_i \pm 2hf'_i + 2h^2 f''_i \pm \dfrac{4h^3}{3}f'''_i + \dfrac{2h^4}{3}f^{(4)}_i + O(h^5) \]
  2. Form linear combination to cancel \(f'\) and \(f'''\) terms:
    \(-f_{i+2} + 16f_{i+1} - 30f_i + 16f_{i-1} - f_{i-2}\)
  3. Divide by \(12h^2\):
    \[f''_i = \dfrac{-f_{i+2} + 16f_{i+1} - 30f_i + 16f_{i-1} - f_{i-2}}{12h^2} + O(h^4) \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{12h^2}\left[-f_{i+2} + 16f_{i+1} - 30f_i + 16f_{i-1} - f_{i-2}\right]\) | Correct option: (A)

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
options: P is a homogeneous ODE and Q is an exact ODE.
P is a homogeneous ODE and Q is not an exact ODE.
P is a nonhomogeneous ODE and Q is an exact ODE.

questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Differential Equations | Classification of First-Order ODEs

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    \(P:\displaystyle\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x^4 + 3x^2y^2 + 2y^4}{x^3 y}\)
    \(Q:\displaystyle\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{y^2}{x^2}\)
  • Aim: Classify P and Q with respect to homogeneity and exactness.

Core Concepts:

  • Homogeneous ODE: RHS is a homogeneous function of degree zero, i.e., replacing \((x, y) \to (tx, ty)\) leaves the expression unchanged.
  • Exact ODE: In \(M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\) form, exactness requires \(\dfrac{\partial M}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial N}{\partial x}\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. For P — Homogeneity check:
    Numerator degree = 4, denominator degree = 4 → overall degree 0.
    Replace \((x, y) \to (tx, ty)\):
    \[\dfrac{(tx)^4 + 3(tx)^2(ty)^2 + 2(ty)^4}{(tx)^3(ty)} = \dfrac{t^4(\cdots)}{t^4 x^3 y} = \dfrac{x^4 + 3x^2y^2 + 2y^4}{x^3 y} \]
    Expression unchanged. \(\therefore\) P is homogeneous.
  2. For Q — Exactness check:
    Rewrite: \(y^2\,dx + x^2\,dy = 0\) → \(M = y^2\), \(N = x^2\).
    \[\dfrac{\partial M}{\partial y} = 2y, \quad \dfrac{\partial N}{\partial x} = 2x \]
    \(2y \neq 2x\) in general. \(\therefore\) Q is not exact.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: P is a homogeneous ODE and Q is not an exact ODE | Correct option: (B)

questions.question:
A 3 m long, horizontal, rigid, uniform beam PQ has negligible mass. The beam is subjected to a 3 kN concentrated vertically downward force at 1 m from P, as shown in the figure. The beam is resting on vertical linear springs at the ends P and Q. For the spring at the end P, the spring constant \( K_P = 100 \) kN/m.



If the beam DOES NOT rotate under the application of the force and displaces only vertically, the value of the spring constant \( K_Q \) (in kN/m) for the spring at the end Q is
questions.explanation:
Strength of Materials | Rigid Beams on Elastic Supports (Spring Stiffness)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Beam length \(L = 3\text{ m}\); concentrated vertical load \(P = 3\text{ kN}\) at 1 m from P; spring stiffness at P, \(K_P = 100\text{ kN/m}\); beam rigid, uniform, negligible mass; pure vertical translation (no rotation).
  • Aim: Find the value of spring constant \(K_Q\) (kN/m) at Q.

Core Concepts:

  • Compatibility: For a rigid beam with zero rotation, vertical deflection at P equals deflection at Q (\(\delta_P = \delta_Q = \delta\)).
  • Hooke's Law: Spring reaction \(F = K \times \delta\).
  • Static equilibrium: \(\sum F_y = 0\) and \(\sum M = 0\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Let uniform downward deflection of rigid beam \(= \delta\) (m).
    Reaction at P: \(F_P = 100\delta\) kN (upward).
    Reaction at Q: \(F_Q = K_Q \delta\) kN (upward).
  2. Moment equilibrium about P:
    \[3 \times 1 = F_Q \times 3 \implies F_Q = 1\text{ kN} \]
  3. Vertical force equilibrium:
    \[F_P = 3 - 1 = 2\text{ kN} \]
  4. Find \(\delta\) from spring at P:
    \[\delta = \dfrac{F_P}{K_P} = \dfrac{2}{100} = 0.02\text{ m} \]

questions.question:
For a thin-walled section shown in the figure, points P, Q, and R are located on the major bending axis X – X of the section. Point Q is located on the web whereas point S is located at the intersection of the web and the top flange of the section.



Qualitatively, the shear center of the section lies at
questions.explanation:
Strength of Materials | Thin-Walled Open Sections | Shear Centre

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Thin-walled section with top/bottom flanges having 6 cm projection on left of web and 3 cm on right; major bending axis X–X; points P (left), Q (on web), R (right) on X–X; S at top flange–web intersection.
  • Aim: Qualitative location of the shear centre.

Core Concepts:

Shear centre is the unique point where an applied transverse shear force produces pure bending with zero torsion (net torque from shear flows = 0). For open thin-walled sections, horizontal shear flow in flanges is proportional to distance from the free end — unequal flange projections create an unbalanced torsional couple.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Flanges are asymmetric: left overhang = 6 cm, right overhang = 3 cm.
  2. Under vertical shear, shear flow in flanges is proportional to flange length from free end.
  3. Longer left flange (6 cm) produces a larger horizontal shear force and larger moment arm than the shorter right flange (3 cm).
  4. Net torsional couple is clockwise; to nullify this torque, the line of action of total vertical shear must shift to the right of the web (towards the shorter flange side).
  5. Among the given options, this shift places the shear centre at point R on the major axis X–X.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: R | Correct option: (C)

questions.question: A simply supported, uniformly loaded, two-way slab panel is torsionally unrestrained. The effective span lengths along the short span (x) and long span (y) directions of the panel are \( l_x \) and \( l_y \), respectively. The design moments for the reinforcements along the x and y directions are \( M_{ux} \) and \( M_{uy} \), respectively. By using Rankine-Grashoff method, the ratio \( M_{ux}/M_{uy} \) is proportional to
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Design | Two-Way Slabs (IS 456:2000)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Simply supported, uniformly loaded, torsionally unrestrained two-way slab; effective spans \(l_x\) (short) and \(l_y\) (long); moments \(M_{ux}\) and \(M_{uy}\).
  • Aim: Find the ratio \(M_{ux}/M_{uy}\) by the Rankine-Grashoff method.

Core Concepts:

Rankine-Grashoff method (classical approximate approach for torsionally unrestrained slabs): load sharing is based on equal central deflection condition, giving \(w_x / w_y = l_y^4 / l_x^4\). Moments are then \(M_{ux} = w_x l_x^2 / 8\) and \(M_{uy} = w_y l_y^2 / 8\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Load ratio from equal deflection:
    \[\dfrac{w_x}{w_y} = \left(\dfrac{l_y}{l_x}\right)^4 \]
  2. Moment expressions:
    \[M_{ux} = \dfrac{w_x l_x^2}{8}, \quad M_{uy} = \dfrac{w_y l_y^2}{8} \]
  3. Compute ratio:
    \[\dfrac{M_{ux}}{M_{uy}} = \dfrac{w_x}{w_y} \times \dfrac{l_x^2}{l_y^2} = \left(\dfrac{l_y}{l_x}\right)^4 \times \dfrac{l_x^2}{l_y^2} = \left(\dfrac{l_y}{l_x}\right)^2 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\mathbf{(l_y/l_x)^2}\) | Correct option: (D)

Various stresses in jointed plain concrete pavement with slab size of 3.5 m × 4.5 m are denoted as follows:

Wheel load stress at interior = \( S_{wl}^i \)
Wheel load stress at edge = \( S_{wl}^e \)
Wheel load stress at corner = \( S_{wl}^c \)
Warping stress at interior = \( S_t^i \)
Warping stress at edge = \( S_t^e \)
Warping stress at corner = \( S_t^c \)
Frictional stress between slab and supporting layer = \( S_f \)

The critical stress combination in the concrete slab during a summer midnight is
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Design of Rigid Pavements (Stresses in Jointed Plain Concrete Pavement)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Slab size 3.5 m × 4.5 m; stresses defined: \(S_{wl}^i, S_{wl}^e, S_{wl}^c\) (wheel load at interior, edge, corner); \(S_t^i, S_t^e, S_t^c\) (warping); \(S_f\) (friction).
  • Aim: Identify critical stress combination during summer midnight.

Core Concepts:

Westergaard's theory (modified by IRC:58-2015): Summer midnight → negative temperature gradient (top cooler than bottom → slab curls upward at edges/corners). At a corner: free edge → \(S_f = 0\) (no frictional restraint). Critical tensile stress at top fibre = \(S_{wl}^c + S_t^c\) (both additive).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Summer midnight → negative gradient → upward curl at corners → tensile warping stress at top.
  2. Wheel load at corner → tensile stress at top fibre → \(S_{wl}^c\).
  3. Corner is a free edge → friction stress \(S_f = 0\).
  4. Critical combination: \(S_{wl}^c + S_t^c\) (both act at same fibre, no friction term).

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\mathbf{S_{wl}^c + S_t^c}\) | Correct option: (A)

Core Concepts:

When repeated measurements of equal precision are made, the most probable value is the arithmetic mean (principle of least squares for equal weights).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  • Aim: Compute shape factor (rounded to 2 decimal places).

Core Concepts:

Shape factor: \(f = Z_p / Z_e\), where \(Z_p\) = plastic section modulus. The plastic neutral axis (PNA) divides the section into two equal half-areas (\(A/2\) each). Relevant provision: IS 800:2007, Clause 7.1.2 & Annex F.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total area:
    \[A = t(a + b - t) = 3(15 + 12 - 3) = 72\text{ cm}^2 \implies A/2 = 36\text{ cm}^2 \]
  2. Locate PNA: Full horizontal leg area \(= 12 \times 3 = 36\text{ cm}^2 = A/2\). PNA lies exactly at the top of the horizontal leg (\(y_p = 3\text{ cm}\) from bottom).
  3. Plastic moment contributions:
    • Below PNA (horizontal leg): centroid at 1.5 cm from bottom; lever arm = 1.5 cm
      \(M_{below} = 36 \times 1.5 = 54\text{ cm}^3\)
    • Above PNA (vertical web, 12 cm × 3 cm): centroid at 9 cm from bottom; lever arm = 6 cm
      \(M_{above} = 36 \times 6 = 216\text{ cm}^3\)
  4. Plastic section modulus:
    \[Z_p = 54 + 216 = 270\text{ cm}^3 \]
  5. Shape factor:
    \[f = \dfrac{Z_p}{Z_e} = \dfrac{270}{150.92} = 1.79 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.79 | Accepted range: [1.75 to 1.85]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q34

questions.question: A reinforced concrete pile of 10 m length and 0.7 m diameter is embedded in a saturated pure clay with unit cohesion of 50 kPa. If the adhesion factor is 0.5, the net ultimate uplift pullout capacity (in kN) of the pile is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Pile Foundations (Uplift Capacity in Clay)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Pile length \(L = 10\text{ m}\), diameter \(D = 0.7\text{ m}\); saturated clay \(c_u = 50\text{ kPa}\); adhesion factor \(\alpha = 0.5\).
  • Aim: Net ultimate uplift pullout capacity (kN, nearest integer).

Core Concepts:

For uplift in cohesive soil, net ultimate capacity = skin adhesion only (end resistance neglected):
\[Q_u = \alpha \cdot c_u \cdot (\pi D L) \]
Relevant provision: IS 2911 (Part 1/Sec 1):2010, Clause 7.3.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Adhesion strength:
    \[\alpha \cdot c_u = 0.5 \times 50 = 25\text{ kPa} \]
  2. Shaft surface area:
    \[\pi D L = \pi \times 0.7 \times 10 = 21.991\text{ m}^2 \]
  3. Uplift capacity:
    \[Q_u = 25 \times 21.991 = 549.78\text{ kN} \approx 550\text{ kN} \]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q35
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 2 m wide rectangular channel is carrying a discharge of 30 m³/s at a bed slope of 1 in 300. Assuming the energy correction factor as 1.1 and acceleration due to gravity as 10 m/s², the critical depth of flow (in meters) is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Critical Depth with Energy Correction)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Rectangular channel width \(B = 2\text{ m}\), discharge \(Q = 30\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), energy correction factor \(\alpha = 1.1\), \(g = 10\text{ m/s}^2\).
  • Aim: Critical depth \(y_c\) (m, rounded to 2 decimal places).

Core Concepts:

Critical flow condition (\(dE/dy = 0\)) with energy correction factor \(\alpha\):
\[\alpha \dfrac{Q^2 B}{g A^3} = 1 \]
For a rectangular channel this simplifies to:
\[y_c = \left(\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{g B^2}\right)^{1/3} \]
Note: Omitting \(\alpha\) is a common pitfall.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. \[\alpha Q^2 = 1.1 \times 30^2 = 1.1 \times 900 = 990 \]
  2. \[g B^2 = 10 \times 2^2 = 40 \]
  3. \[\dfrac{\alpha Q^2}{g B^2} = \dfrac{990}{40} = 24.75 \]
  4. \[y_c = (24.75)^{1/3} \approx 2.91\text{ m} \]
    (Verification: \(2.914^3 \approx 24.75\) ✓)
  5. Without \(\alpha\), \(y_c \approx 2.88\text{ m}\); \(\alpha > 1\) increases \(y_c\) as expected.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 2.91 m | Accepted range: [2.88 to 2.94]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q36
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question: In a sample of 100 heart patients, each patient has 80% chance of having a heart attack without medicine X. It is clinically known that medicine X reduces the probability of having a heart attack by 50%. Medicine X is taken by 50 of these 100 patients. The probability that a randomly selected patient, out of the 100 patients, takes medicine X and has a heart attack is
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Probability

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Total patients \(N = 100\)
    Probability of heart attack without medicine \(P(A|M') = 0.80\) (or 80%)
    Medicine reduces heart attack probability by 50%
    Patients taking medicine \(N_M = 50\)
  • Aim: Find the probability that a randomly selected patient takes medicine X AND has a heart attack, i.e., \(P(M \cap A)\).

Core Concepts:

Conditional Probability: The probability of two dependent events occurring together is given by the general multiplication rule: \(P(M \cap A) = P(M) \times P(A|M)\).

Percentage Reduction: If a base probability \(P_0\) is reduced by \(x\%\), the new probability is \(P_{new} = P_0 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{x}{100}\right)\).

Solution Method:

  • First, determine the baseline probability of taking the medicine \(P(M)\).
  • Second, calculate the conditional probability of having a heart attack given that the medicine is taken, \(P(A|M)\).
  • Finally, multiply both probabilities.
  • Note: A common pitfall here is confusing "reduces the probability to 50%" with "reduces by 50%." Here, the reduction is relative to the baseline 80% probability.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate \(P(M)\): 50 out of 100 patients take the medicine.
    \[P(M) = \dfrac{50}{100} = 0.5 \]
  2. Calculate \(P(A|M)\): The medicine reduces the baseline 80% probability by 50%.
    \[P(A|M) = 0.80 \times (1 - 0.50) = 0.40 \]
  3. Calculate Joint Probability \(P(M \cap A)\):
    \[P(M \cap A) = P(M) \times P(A|M) \]\[P(M \cap A) = 0.5 \times 0.40 = 0.20 \]
    Convert to percentage: \(0.20 \times 100\% = 20\%\)

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 20% | Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A linearly elastic beam of length \( 2l \) with flexural rigidity \( EI \) has negligible mass. A massless spring with a spring constant \( k \) and a rigid block of mass \( m \) are attached to the beam as shown in the figure.



The natural frequency of this system is
questions.explanation:
Structural Dynamics | Natural Frequency

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Beam length \(= 2l\)
    Flexural rigidity \(= EI\)
    Spring constant \(= k\)
    Rigid block mass \(= m\)
    The visual layout implies the spring and the beam's midspan undergo the same vertical deflection when the mass \(m\) oscillates.
  • Aim: Find the natural frequency of the system.

Core Concepts:

Equivalent Stiffness (\(k_{eq}\)): For a single degree of freedom (SDOF) undamped system, natural frequency \(\omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{eq}}{m}}\).

Beam Stiffness (\(k_b\)): The stiffness of a simply supported beam subject to a central point load is derived from its deflection formula: \(\Delta = \dfrac{PL^3}{48EI}\). Thus, \(k_b = \dfrac{P}{\Delta} = \dfrac{48EI}{L^3}\).

Spring Configuration: Since the spring and beam are connected such that they deform by the same amount under the dynamic action of the mass, they act in parallel. For parallel springs, \(k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2\).

Solution Method:

  • Substitute the given length \(L = 2l\) into the beam stiffness formula.
  • Add the beam's equivalent stiffness to the spring constant \(k\).
  • Plug the combined stiffness into the natural frequency equation.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Determine beam stiffness \(k_b\): Total length \(L = 2l\).
    \[k_b = \dfrac{48EI}{(2l)^3} = \dfrac{48EI}{8l^3} = \dfrac{6EI}{l^3} \]
  2. Determine equivalent stiffness \(k_{eq}\): Since they are in parallel,
    \[k_{eq} = k + k_b = k + \dfrac{6EI}{l^3} = \dfrac{kl^3 + 6EI}{l^3} \]
  3. Calculate natural frequency \(\omega_n\):
    \[\omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{k_{eq}}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{kl^3 + 6EI}{l^3}}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{kl^3 + 6EI}{ml^3}} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\omega_n = \sqrt{\dfrac{kl^3 + 6EI}{ml^3}}\) | Correct option: (A)

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?

structuredOptions.text: Both P and Q are FALSE
structuredOptions.html: Both P and Q are FALSE

questions.explanation:
Construction Management | Project Crashing

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application/Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Normal time \(t_n = 15\) days, Normal cost \(C_n = \text{Rs. } 30{,}000\)
    Crash time \(t_c = 12\) days, Crash cost \(C_c = \text{Rs. } 54{,}000\)
    Statement P: Indirect cost \(= \text{Rs. } 8{,}500\text{/day}\)
    Statement Q: Indirect cost \(= \text{Rs. } 10{,}000\text{/day}\)
  • Aim: Determine the validity of statements P and Q regarding the economic feasibility of crashing.

Core Concepts:

Cost Slope: The cost to expedite an activity by one day.
\[\text{Cost Slope} = \dfrac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{C_c - C_n}{t_n - t_c} \]

Economic Crashing: Crashing an activity is economically advisable if the cost to crash 1 day (Cost Slope) is \(\leq\) the savings from indirect costs per day.

Solution Method:

Important Note: The official GATE answer key marks this question as MTA (Marks to All). The critical engineering trap here is: while the mathematical cost slope is Rs. 8,000/day, crashing a critical activity by 3 days does not guarantee the overall project duration will decrease by 3 days (another parallel path might become critical after day 1 or 2). Without the full network diagram to verify that no other paths become critical, it cannot be definitively stated that the project saves the full indirect costs. Hence, the question is technically incomplete, leading to MTA.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Cost Slope:
    \[\text{Cost Slope} = \dfrac{54000 - 30000}{15 - 12} = \dfrac{24000}{3} = 8000 \text{ Rs/day} \]
  2. Analyze Statement P: Indirect cost saving \(= 8{,}500 \text{ Rs/day}\).
    Since Cost Slope (\(8{,}000\)) \(<\) Indirect Savings (\(8{,}500\)), crashing is theoretically economical. (P would be TRUE)
  3. Analyze Statement Q: Indirect cost saving \(= 10{,}000 \text{ Rs/day}\).
    Since Cost Slope (\(8{,}000\)) \(<\) Indirect Savings (\(10{,}000\)), crashing is theoretically economical. (Q would be TRUE)

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Theoretically Option (A), but officially MTA due to missing network diagram context | Correct option: MTA

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A homogeneous, prismatic, linearly elastic steel bar fixed at both the ends has a slenderness ratio (\( l/r \)) of 105, where \( l \) is the bar length and \( r \) is the radius of gyration. The coefficient of thermal expansion of steel is \( 12 \times 10^{-6} /°C \). Consider the effective length of the steel bar as \( 0.5l \) and neglect the self-weight of the bar.

The differential increase in temperature (rounded off to the nearest integer) at which the bar buckles is
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Thermal Stresses & Column Buckling

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Fixed-fixed steel bar
    Slenderness ratio \(\dfrac{l}{r} = 105\)
    Thermal expansion coefficient \(\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6} \text{ /}^\circ\text{C}\)
    Effective length \(L_{eff} = 0.5l\)
  • Aim: Find the differential temperature \(\Delta T\) at which the bar buckles.

Core Concepts:

Thermal Stress: A bar prevented from expanding will develop a compressive thermal stress:
\[\sigma_{th} = E \alpha \Delta T \]

Euler's Buckling Stress: The critical compressive stress at which a slender column buckles is:
\[\sigma_{cr} = \dfrac{\pi^2 E}{\lambda_{eff}^2} \]
where \(\lambda_{eff} = \dfrac{L_{eff}}{r}\).

Buckling Condition: Buckling occurs when the induced thermal stress equals the critical buckling stress (\(\sigma_{th} = \sigma_{cr}\)). Note that Young's Modulus (\(E\)) mathematically cancels out.

Solution Method:

  • Calculate the effective slenderness ratio \(\lambda_{eff}\).
  • Equate \(\sigma_{th}\) and \(\sigma_{cr}\) and solve for \(\Delta T\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate effective slenderness ratio: Given \(\dfrac{l}{r} = 105\) and \(L_{eff} = 0.5l\).
    \[\lambda_{eff} = \dfrac{L_{eff}}{r} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{l}{r} = 0.5 \times 105 = 52.5 \]
  2. Equate thermal and buckling stresses:
    \[E \alpha \Delta T = \dfrac{\pi^2 E}{\lambda_{eff}^2} \]\[\alpha \Delta T = \dfrac{\pi^2}{52.5^2} \]
  3. Solve for \(\Delta T\):
    \[12 \times 10^{-6} \times \Delta T = \dfrac{\pi^2}{2756.25} \]\[12 \times 10^{-6} \times \Delta T = 0.0035805 \]\[\Delta T = \dfrac{0.0035805}{12 \times 10^{-6}} = 298.375 ^\circ\text{C} \]
    Round to the nearest integer: \(\Delta T \approx 298 ^\circ\text{C}\)

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(298 ^\circ\text{C}\) | Correct option: (A)

Consider the statements P and Q related to the analysis/design of retaining walls.

P: When a rough retaining wall moves toward the backfill, the wall friction force/resistance mobilizes in upward direction along the wall.

Q: Most of the earth pressure theories calculate the earth pressure due to surcharge by neglecting the actual distribution of stresses due to surcharge.

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
options: Both P and Q are TRUE
P is TRUE and Q is FALSE
Both P and Q are FALSE
P is FALSE and Q is TRUE

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Both P and Q are TRUE
structuredOptions.html: Both P and Q are TRUE

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: P is TRUE and Q is FALSE
structuredOptions.html: P is TRUE and Q is FALSE

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: Both P and Q are FALSE
structuredOptions.html: Both P and Q are FALSE

structuredOptions.label: D

structuredOptions.html: P is FALSE and Q is TRUE

questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Earth Pressure Theories

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data:
    Statement P: In a passive state (wall moves toward backfill), wall friction mobilizes upward.
    Statement Q: Most theories neglect actual stress distribution for surcharge earth pressure.
  • Aim: Identify whether statements P and Q are TRUE or FALSE.

Core Concepts:

Passive Earth Pressure & Wall Friction: When a retaining wall is pushed into the backfill (passive case), the soil wedge is forced upward and outward along the failure plane. Because the soil wedge moves upward relative to the wall, the friction exerted by the wall on the soil is downward to oppose the movement. Therefore, the wall friction resistance mobilized along the wall acts downward.

Surcharge Loading: Standard theories (Rankine/Coulomb) simplify a uniform surcharge \(q\) as a constant lateral earth pressure increase (\(\Delta p = K \cdot q\)) throughout the entire depth, completely ignoring the non-linear Boussinesq or Westergaard elastic stress distribution bulbs.

Solution Method:

  • Evaluate P: The relative motion of the soil wedge is upward. Therefore, the frictional resistance acting on the soil is downward. Statement P claims it is upward, so it is FALSE.
  • Evaluate Q: Standard earth pressure theories indeed simplify surcharge effects by treating them as uniform rectangular distributions, neglecting the exact elastic stress variations. So, statement Q is TRUE.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze Statement P: Wall moves toward backfill \(\rightarrow\) Passive state. Soil moves upward relative to the wall. Frictional resistance (acting to oppose soil movement) is downward. Statement P says "upward", so P is FALSE.
  2. Analyze Statement Q: Theories calculate pressure due to surcharge assuming uniform lateral pressure increase, neglecting actual stress distributions. Q is TRUE.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: P is FALSE and Q is TRUE | Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q41
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A round-bottom triangular lined canal is to be laid at a slope of 1 in 1500, to carry a discharge of 25 m³/s. The side slopes of the canal cross-section are to be kept at 1.25H : 1V. If Manning’s roughness coefficient is 0.013, the flow depth (in meters) will be in the range of
questions.explanation:
Open Channel Flow | Lined Canals

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Discharge, \(Q = 25\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\)
    Bed slope, \(S = 1/1500\)
    Side slopes, \(m = 1.25\text{ (H)} : 1\text{ (V)}\)
    Manning's roughness, \(n = 0.013\)
    Section: Round-bottom triangular lined canal
  • Aim: Determine the normal flow depth, \(y\) (in meters).

Core Concepts:

According to IS 10430 (Criteria for Design of Lined Canals), a round-bottom triangular canal is designed such that the circular arc at the bed is tangential to the straight side slopes, and its center lies at the water surface. This geometry forms the "best hydraulic section" for a triangle.

Let \(\theta\) be the angle the side slope makes with the vertical (in radians): \(\tan\theta = \text{Horizontal} / \text{Vertical} = m = 1.25\)

  • Cross-sectional Area: \(A = y^2(\theta + \tan\theta)\)
  • Wetted Perimeter: \(P = 2y(\theta + \tan\theta)\)
  • Hydraulic Radius: \(R = A/P = y/2\)
  • Manning's Equation: \(Q = \dfrac{1}{n} A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate the angle \(\theta\):
    \[\tan\theta = 1.25 \Rightarrow \theta = \arctan(1.25) = 0.8961\text{ radians} \]
  2. Express Area and Perimeter in terms of \(y\):
    Geometric constant \(k = (\theta + \tan\theta) = 0.8961 + 1.25 = 2.1461\)
    \[A = 2.1461\, y^2, \quad R = y/2 = 0.5y \]
  3. Apply Manning's Equation:
    \[25 = \dfrac{1}{0.013} \times (2.1461\, y^2) \times (0.5y)^{2/3} \times \left(\dfrac{1}{1500}\right)^{1/2} \]\[25 = 76.923 \times 2.1461 \times 0.630\, y^{2/3} \times 0.02582\, y^2 \]\[25 = 2.684\, y^{8/3} \]
  4. Solve for \(y\):
    \[y^{8/3} = \dfrac{25}{2.684} = 9.314 \]\[y = (9.314)^{3/8} = 2.404\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(y \approx 2.40\text{ m}\) | Accepted key range: [2.39 to 2.42]

questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Treatment (Filtration)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Anthracite: \(S_a = 1.50\)
    Silica Sand: \(S_s = 2.60\), \(d_s = 0.20\text{ mm}\)
    Ilmenite Sand: \(S_i = 4.20\)
    Regime: Slow discrete settling (Stokes' law applies), spherical particles.
  • Aim: Find diameter conditions for anthracite (\(d_a\)) and ilmenite (\(d_i\)) to achieve desired stratification after backwashing: Top = Anthracite, Middle = Silica, Bottom = Ilmenite.

Core Concepts:

During backwashing, particles expand and settle. For standard stratification, particles must settle according to their settling velocities (\(V_s\)):
\[V_{s,\text{anthracite}} < V_{s,\text{silica}} < V_{s,\text{ilmenite}} \]

Stokes' Law: \(V_s = \dfrac{g(S-1)d^2}{18\nu}\)
Since \(g\) and \(\nu\) are constant: \(V_s \propto (S-1)d^2\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate the settling factor for Silica Sand (Middle Layer):
    \[\text{Factor} = (S_s - 1)d_s^2 = (2.60 - 1) \times (0.20)^2 = 1.6 \times 0.04 = 0.064 \]
  2. Condition for Anthracite (Top Layer): Must settle slower than silica:
    \[(S_a - 1)d_a^2 < 0.064 \]\[(1.50 - 1)d_a^2 < 0.064 \Rightarrow 0.5\,d_a^2 < 0.064 \Rightarrow d_a^2 < 0.128 \]\[d_a < \sqrt{0.128} \approx 0.358\text{ mm} \]
  3. Condition for Ilmenite (Bottom Layer): Must settle faster than silica:
    \[(S_i - 1)d_i^2 > 0.064 \]\[(4.20 - 1)d_i^2 > 0.064 \Rightarrow 3.2\,d_i^2 > 0.064 \Rightarrow d_i^2 > 0.02 \]\[d_i > \sqrt{0.02} \approx 0.141\text{ mm} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(d_a < 0.358\text{ mm}\) and \(d_i > 0.141\text{ mm}\) | Correct option: (A)

questions.question:
Three vectors \( \vec{p} \), \( \vec{q} \), and \( \vec{r} \) are given as

\[\vec{p} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k} \]

Which of the following is/are CORRECT?
questions.explanation:

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: \(\vec{p} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\),   \(\vec{q} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\),   \(\vec{r} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}\)
  • Aim: Identify mathematically correct vector identities from given options (MSQ).

Core Concepts:

Jacobi Identity: \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) + \vec{b}\times(\vec{c}\times\vec{a}) + \vec{c}\times(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}) = \vec{0}\)   (Universally true)

Vector Triple Product (BAC-CAB Rule): \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) = (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b} - (\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}\)   (Universally true)

Scalar Triple Product \([\vec{a},\vec{b},\vec{c}]\): \(\vec{a}\cdot(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})\). Represents the volume of the parallelepiped. If vectors are coplanar, it equals 0.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Evaluate (A): This is the standard Jacobi Identity. It is universally TRUE.
  2. Evaluate (B): This is the standard Vector Triple Product expansion. It is universally TRUE.
  3. Evaluate (C): Cross product is not generally associative.
    \(\vec{p}\times(\vec{q}\times\vec{r}) \neq (\vec{p}\times\vec{q})\times\vec{r}\).   FALSE.
  4. Evaluate (D): \(\vec{r}\cdot(\vec{p}\times\vec{q}) = (\vec{q}\times\vec{p})\cdot\vec{r}\)
    LHS \(= [\vec{r}, \vec{p}, \vec{q}]\).   RHS \(= [\vec{q}, \vec{p}, \vec{r}] = -[\vec{r}, \vec{p}, \vec{q}]\).
    This implies \([\vec{r}, \vec{p}, \vec{q}] = -[\vec{r}, \vec{p}, \vec{q}]\), which is only possible if \([\vec{r}, \vec{p}, \vec{q}] = 0\).

    Check for linear dependence: Notice that
    \[\vec{p} + \vec{q} = (1+1)\hat{i} + (1+2)\hat{j} + (1+3)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k} = \vec{r} \]
    Since \(\vec{r}\) is a linear combination of \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\), the three vectors are coplanar. Thus, their scalar triple product is exactly 0, making \(0 = -0\). Statement (D) is TRUE for these specific vectors.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Correct options: (A), (B), (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q47
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
The expression for computing the effective interest rate (\( i_{eff} \)) using continuous compounding for a nominal interest rate of 5% is

\[i_{eff} = \lim_{m \to \infty} \left(1 + \dfrac{0.05}{m}\right)^m - 1 \]

The effective interest rate (in percentage) is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Economics | Continuous Compounding

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Nominal interest rate \(r = 5\%\) or \(0.05\). Continuous compounding limit expression for effective interest rate \(i_{eff}\).
  • Aim: Compute the effective interest rate in percentage, rounded to 2 decimal places.

Core Concepts:

Continuous Compounding Limit: When the number of compounding periods per year (\(m\)) approaches infinity, the discrete compounding formula transitions into an exponential function based on Euler's number (\(e\)).

Fundamental Mathematical Limit:\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \dfrac{a}{x}\right)^{x} = e^{a} \]

Effective Interest Rate Formula: For continuous compounding: \(i_{eff} = e^{r} - 1\), where \(r\) is the nominal annual interest rate in decimal form.

Solution Method:

  1. Identify the nominal rate \(r\) from the given limit expression.
  2. Substitute \(r\) into the continuous compounding formula.
  3. Evaluate the exponential term.
  4. Convert the resulting decimal to a percentage.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. From the given limit expression \(i_{eff} = \lim_{m \to \infty} \left(1 + \dfrac{0.05}{m}\right)^{m} - 1\), the nominal interest rate \(r = 0.05\).
  2. Applying the standard limit identity:
    \[i_{eff} = e^{0.05} - 1 \]
  3. Calculate the value of \(e^{0.05}\):
    \[e^{0.05} \approx 1.051271 \]
  4. Calculate \(i_{eff}\) in decimal form:
    \[i_{eff} = 1.051271 - 1 = 0.051271 \]
  5. Convert to percentage and round to 2 decimal places:
    \[0.051271 \times 100 = 5.1271\% \approx 5.13\% \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 5.13% | Accepted key range: [5.11 to 5.15]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q48

questions.question:
Consider two matrices \( \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( \mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \).

The determinant of the matrix \( \mathbf{AB} \) is _________ (in integer).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Linear Algebra

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) of order \(2 \times 3\), Matrix \(\mathbf{B}\) of order \(3 \times 2\).
  • Aim: Find the determinant of the product matrix \(\mathbf{AB}\) as an integer.

Core Concepts:

Matrix Multiplication: To multiply an \(m \times n\) matrix by an \(n \times p\) matrix, the inner dimensions must match. The resulting matrix will have dimensions \(m \times p\).

Determinant of a 2×2 Matrix: For a matrix \(\mathbf{C} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the determinant is \(|\mathbf{C}| = ad - bc\).

Pitfall to avoid: Do not attempt to calculate \(|\mathbf{A}| \times |\mathbf{B}|\), as determinants are only defined for square matrices.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Define the given matrices:
    \[\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \]A \(2 \times 3\) matrix multiplied by a \(3 \times 2\) matrix yields a \(2 \times 2\) matrix.
  2. Compute matrix \(\mathbf{AB}\):
    • Row 1, Col 1: \((2 \times -1) + (1 \times 2) + (4 \times 1) = -2 + 2 + 4 = 4\)
    • Row 1, Col 2: \((2 \times 0) + (1 \times 3) + (4 \times 4) = 0 + 3 + 16 = 19\)
    • Row 2, Col 1: \((1 \times -1) + (0 \times 2) + (3 \times 1) = -1 + 0 + 3 = 2\)
    • Row 2, Col 2: \((1 \times 0) + (0 \times 3) + (3 \times 4) = 0 + 0 + 12 = 12\)
  3. Form the resulting matrix \(\mathbf{AB}\):
    \[\mathbf{AB} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 19 \\ 2 & 12 \end{bmatrix} \]
  4. Calculate the determinant \(|\mathbf{AB}|\):
    \[|\mathbf{AB}| = (4 \times 12) - (19 \times 2) = 48 - 38 = 10 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 10 | Accepted key range: [10 to 10]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q49
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
For the 6 m long horizontal cantilever beam PQR shown in the figure, Q is the midpoint. Segment PQ of the beam has flexural rigidity EI = \( 2 \times 10^5 \) kN.m² whereas the segment QR has infinite flexural rigidity. Segment QR is subjected to uniformly distributed, vertically downward load of 5 kN/m.



The magnitude of the vertical displacement (in mm) at point Q is _________ (rounded off to 3 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Deflection of Beams

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Total beam length PQR = 6 m.
    Segment PQ length = 3 m, flexural rigidity \(EI = 2 \times 10^5\text{ kN.m}^2\).
    Segment QR length = 3 m, infinite flexural rigidity (\(EI = \infty\)).
    Load on QR = 5 kN/m UDL acting vertically downward.
  • Aim: Determine the vertical displacement at point Q in mm, rounded to 3 decimal places.

Core Concepts:

Rigid Body Mechanics: Segment QR has infinite flexural rigidity — it will not bend or deform, acting as a rigid lever arm transferring applied loads directly to point Q.

Equivalent Nodal Loads: A load on a rigid attachment can be statically transferred to the elastic support point (Q) as an equivalent point load and a concentrated bending moment.

Superposition Theorem: Total deflection at Q = sum of individual deflections caused by the equivalent point load and moment acting independently on cantilever PQ.

Standard Cantilever Deflection Formulas (Euler-Bernoulli Beam Theory):

  • Deflection due to point load \(W\) at free end: \(\delta_W = \dfrac{WL^3}{3EI}\)
  • Deflection due to concentrated moment \(M\) at free end: \(\delta_M = \dfrac{ML^2}{2EI}\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze Rigid Segment QR:
    UDL \(= 5\text{ kN/m}\) over length 3 m.
    Total downward force: \(W = 5 \times 3 = 15\text{ kN}\).
    Resultant acts at centroid of UDL, i.e., \(1.5\text{ m}\) from Q.
  2. Transfer Load to Point Q:
    Vertical point load: \(V_Q = 15\text{ kN}\) (downward).
    Moment at Q: \(M_Q = 15 \times 1.5 = 22.5\text{ kN.m}\) (clockwise, causing downward deflection).
  3. Calculate Deflections for Segment PQ (Length \(L = 3\text{ m}\)):
    Deflection due to point load \(V_Q\):
    \[\delta_1 = \dfrac{V_Q L^3}{3EI} = \dfrac{15 \times 27}{3EI} = \dfrac{135}{EI} \]
    Deflection due to moment \(M_Q\):
    \[\delta_2 = \dfrac{M_Q L^2}{2EI} = \dfrac{22.5 \times 9}{2EI} = \dfrac{101.25}{EI} \]
  4. Total Deflection at Q:
    Both loads cause downward displacement, so they add up:
    \[\delta_Q = \delta_1 + \delta_2 = \dfrac{135}{EI} + \dfrac{101.25}{EI} = \dfrac{236.25}{EI} \]
  5. Substitute Values and Convert Units:
    Given \(EI = 2 \times 10^5\text{ kN.m}^2\):
    \[\delta_Q = \dfrac{236.25}{200000} = 0.00118125\text{ m} \]
    Convert to mm (multiply by 1000):
    \[\delta_Q = 1.18125\text{ mm} \approx 1.181\text{ mm} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 1.181 mm | Accepted key range: [1.176 to 1.186]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The horizontal beam PQRS shown in the figure has a fixed support at point P, an internal hinge at point Q, and a pin support at point R. A concentrated vertically downward load (V) of 10 kN can act at any point over the entire length of the beam.



The maximum magnitude of the moment reaction (in kN.m) that can act at the support P due to V is _________ (in integer).
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Lines & Reactions

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Beam PQRS with total length 30 m (PQ = 15 m, QR = 10 m, RS = 5 m).
    Supports: Fixed at P, internal hinge at Q, pin/roller support at R.
    Load: Moving vertically downward concentrated load \(V = 10\text{ kN}\).
  • Aim: Find the maximum magnitude of the moment reaction at fixed support P (\(M_P\)) in kN.m.

Core Concepts:

Beam Kinematics & Support Reactions: An internal hinge (like Q) cannot transfer bending moment — it can only transfer shear force (vertical reaction). The structure is therefore split into two parts:

  • Cantilever PQ: Fixed at P, provides support to segment QRS at hinge Q.
  • Overhanging Beam QRS: Simply supported by the hinge at Q and the pin at R.

Influence Line Diagrams (ILD): The concept of finding the critical position of a moving load that maximizes a specific reaction or internal force. For a cantilever, the fixed end moment is the applied force multiplied by its perpendicular distance to the fixed support.

Solution Method:

  • Isolate segment QRS and analyze it as a simply supported beam with an overhang.
  • Determine the vertical reaction transferred to hinge Q (\(R_Q\)) for different load positions.
  • Recognize that cantilever PQ only feels the load transferred through hinge Q, or load acting directly on PQ.
  • Calculate \(M_P\) by placing the 10 kN load at critical points (P, Q, R, S) to find the absolute maximum magnitude.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Structural Interaction: Any downward force applied to QRS transfers a fractional downward load to Q. By Newton's Third Law, this acts as a downward point load on the tip of cantilever PQ.
  2. Critical Position 1 — Load at Q:
    The entire 10 kN is directly supported by cantilever PQ at its free end.
    \[M_P = F_Q \times \text{(Distance PQ)} = 10 \times 15 = 150\text{ kN.m (Hogging)} \]
  3. Critical Position 2 — Load between P and Q:
    Let load act at distance \(x\) from P: \(M_P = 10 \times x\). Maximum occurs at \(x = 15\text{ m}\) (at Q), again yielding 150 kN.m.
  4. Critical Position 3 — Load at free end S:
    Analyze FBD of segment QRS. Taking moments about pin support R (\(\sum M_R = 0\)):
    \[R_Q \times 10 - 10 \times 5 = 0 \implies R_Q = 5\text{ kN (upward at Q)} \]
    By Newton's 3rd Law, hinge Q pulls upward on cantilever PQ with 5 kN.
    \[M_P = 5 \times 15 = 75\text{ kN.m (Sagging)} \]
  5. Compare Magnitudes:
    • Load at Q: \(|-150| = 150\text{ kN.m}\)
    • Load at S: \(|+75| = 75\text{ kN.m}\)
    The maximum magnitude is 150 kN.m.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 150 kN.m | Accepted key range: [150 to 150]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question:
A concrete column section of size 300 mm × 500 mm as shown in the figure is subjected to both axial compression and bending along the major axis. The depth of the neutral axis (\( X_u \)) is 1.1 times the depth of the column, as shown.



The maximum compressive strain (\( \varepsilon_c \)) at highly compressive extreme fiber in concrete, where there is no tension in the section, is _________ \( \times 10^{-3} \) (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Reinforced Concrete Design | Limit State of Collapse (Compression)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application/Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Column section dimensions: \(B = 300\text{ mm}\), \(D = 500\text{ mm}\).
    Depth of neutral axis: \(x_u = 1.1D\).
    Subjected to axial compression + bending (no tension in section).
  • Aim: Calculate the maximum compressive strain (\(\epsilon_c\)) at the highly compressed extreme fiber. Format as value \(\times 10^{-3}\), rounded to 2 decimal places.

Core Concepts:

IS 456:2000 Provisions: When \(x_u > D\) (neutral axis lies entirely outside the column cross-section), the entire section is under compression.

Clause 39.1(b): "The maximum compressive strain at the highly compressed extreme fibre in concrete subjected to axial compression and bending and when there is no tension on the section shall be \(0.0035\) minus \(0.75\) times the strain at the least compressed extreme fibre."

Fulcrum/Pivot Point Theorem: Mathematically equivalent to the IS code clause above — the strain profile for \(x_u > D\) always passes through a fixed pivot point where the strain is strictly \(0.002\) at a depth of \(\dfrac{3}{7}D\) from the highly compressed edge.

Solution Method:

  • Assume a linear strain profile across the depth \(x_u\).
  • Set up similar triangles using the highly compressed edge (\(\epsilon_c\) at depth \(x_u\)) and the least compressed edge (\(\epsilon_{min}\) at depth \(x_u - D\)).
  • Apply the IS 456 empirical formula linking \(\epsilon_c\) and \(\epsilon_{min}\).
  • Solve the resulting algebraic equation for \(\epsilon_c\).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Neutral Axis Depth:
    \[x_u = 1.1D = 1.1 \times 500 = 550\text{ mm} \]
  2. Relate Strains via Similar Triangles:
    \[\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{x_u} = \dfrac{\epsilon_{min}}{x_u - D} \]\[\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{1.1D} = \dfrac{\epsilon_{min}}{0.1D} \implies \epsilon_{min} = \epsilon_c \times \dfrac{0.1}{1.1} = \dfrac{\epsilon_c}{11} \]
  3. Apply IS 456:2000 Clause 39.1(b):
    \[\epsilon_c = 0.0035 - 0.75\,\epsilon_{min} \]
  4. Substitute and Solve:
    \[\epsilon_c = 0.0035 - 0.75 \times \dfrac{\epsilon_c}{11} \]\[\epsilon_c + \dfrac{0.75}{11}\,\epsilon_c = 0.0035 \]\[\epsilon_c \left(\dfrac{11.75}{11}\right) = 0.0035 \]\[\epsilon_c = 0.0035 \times \dfrac{11}{11.75} \approx 0.0032766 \]
  5. Format the Output:
    \[0.0032766 = 3.2766 \times 10^{-3} \approx 3.28 \times 10^{-3} \]

Self-Check (Fulcrum Method): Using pivot depth \(\dfrac{3}{7}D\), the similar triangle gives:
\[\dfrac{\epsilon_c}{1.1D} = \dfrac{0.002}{1.1D - \dfrac{3}{7}D} \implies \epsilon_c = 0.002 \times \dfrac{1.1}{0.6714} \approx 0.0032766 \]
Both methods yield identical results, confirming the answer.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.28 \(\times 10^{-3}\) | Accepted key range: [3.20 to 3.40]
