questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A homogeneous earth dam has a maximum water head difference of 15 m between the upstream and downstream sides. A flownet was drawn with the number of potential drops as 10 and the average length of the element as 3 m. Specific gravity of the soil is 2.65. For a factor of safety of 2.0 against piping failure, void ratio of the soil is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Seepage & Flownets

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Maximum water head difference (\(\Delta H\)) = 15 m
    Number of potential drops (\(N_d\)) = 10
    Average length of element (\(\Delta L\)) = 3 m
    Specific gravity (\(G_s\)) = 2.65
    Factor of safety against piping (\(FOS\)) = 2.0
  • Aim: Calculate the void ratio (\(e\)) of the soil.

Core Concepts:

  • Head Loss per Drop: \(\Delta h = \dfrac{\Delta H}{N_d}\)
  • Exit Gradient: \(i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{\Delta L}\)
  • Critical Hydraulic Gradient: \(i_c = \dfrac{G_s - 1}{1 + e}\)
  • Factor of Safety: \(FOS = \dfrac{i_c}{i}\)

Solution Method:

First determine the actual exit gradient. Using the given FOS, back-calculate the required critical hydraulic gradient. Then use the specific gravity to solve for the unknown void ratio.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate head loss per drop:
    \[\Delta h = \dfrac{15}{10} = 1.5\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate maximum exit gradient (\(i\)):
    \[i = \dfrac{\Delta h}{\Delta L} = \dfrac{1.5}{3} = 0.5 \]
  3. Calculate required critical gradient (\(i_c\)):
    \[FOS = \dfrac{i_c}{i} \implies 2.0 = \dfrac{i_c}{0.5} \implies i_c = 1.0 \]
  4. Solve for Void Ratio (\(e\)):
    \[i_c = \dfrac{G_s - 1}{1 + e} \implies 1.0 = \dfrac{2.65 - 1}{1 + e} \]\[1 + e = 1.65 \implies e = 0.65 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(e = 0.65\) | Accepted key range: [0.63 to 0.67]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
The in-situ percentage of voids of a sand deposit is 50%. The maximum and minimum densities of sand determined from the laboratory tests are 1.8 g/cm³ and 1.3 g/cm³, respectively. Assume the specific gravity of sand as 2.7.

The relative density index of the in-situ sand is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Soil Index Properties

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application
  • Given Data:
    In-situ percentage of voids (\(n\)) = 50% = 0.5
    Maximum lab density (\(\rho_{max}\)) = 1.8 g/cm³
    Minimum lab density (\(\rho_{min}\)) = 1.3 g/cm³
    Specific gravity (\(G_s\)) = 2.7
  • Aim: Find the relative density index (\(I_d\)) of the in-situ sand.

Core Concepts:

  • Void Ratio and Porosity: \(e = \dfrac{n}{1 - n}\)
  • Dry Density Relation: \(e = \dfrac{G_s \rho_w}{\rho_d} - 1\)
  • Relative Density: \(I_d = \dfrac{e_{max} - e}{e_{max} - e_{min}}\)

Solution Method:

Convert the given porosity to an in-situ void ratio. Then use the specific gravity relationship to convert maximum and minimum lab densities into minimum and maximum void ratios respectively. Plug into the relative density formula.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate in-situ void ratio (\(e\)):
    \[e = \dfrac{0.5}{1 - 0.5} = 1.0 \]
  2. Calculate minimum void ratio (\(e_{min}\)) — occurs at maximum density:
    \[e_{min} = \dfrac{G_s \rho_w}{\rho_{max}} - 1 = \dfrac{2.7 \times 1.0}{1.8} - 1 = 1.5 - 1 = 0.5 \]
  3. Calculate maximum void ratio (\(e_{max}\)) — occurs at minimum density:
    \[e_{max} = \dfrac{G_s \rho_w}{\rho_{min}} - 1 = \dfrac{2.7 \times 1.0}{1.3} - 1 = 2.0769 - 1 = 1.0769 \]
  4. Calculate Relative Density (\(I_d\)):
    \[I_d = \dfrac{e_{max} - e}{e_{max} - e_{min}} = \dfrac{1.0769 - 1.0}{1.0769 - 0.5} = \dfrac{0.0769}{0.5769} = 0.1333 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.13 (or 13%) | Accepted key range: [0.12 to 0.14] or [12 to 14]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A drained triaxial test was conducted on a saturated sand specimen using a stress-path triaxial testing system. The specimen failed when the axial stress reached a value of 100 kN/m² from an initial confining pressure of 300 kN/m².

The angle of shearing plane (in degrees) with respect to horizontal is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength of Soil

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Drained test on saturated sand. Cohesion \(c' = 0\).
    Initial confining pressure (\(\sigma_c\)) = 300 kN/m².
    Axial stress at failure = 100 kN/m².
  • Aim: Find the angle of the shearing plane with respect to the horizontal.

Core Concepts:

Triaxial Extension Path: The phrasing "axial stress reached a value of 100 from an initial confining pressure of 300" indicates an unloading scenario. The horizontal confining stress remains 300 kN/m², while vertical stress drops to 100 kN/m².

  • Major principal stress: \(\sigma_1 = 300\text{ kN/m}^2\) (acting on the vertical plane)
  • Minor principal stress: \(\sigma_3 = 100\text{ kN/m}^2\) (acting on the horizontal plane)
  • Angle of Internal Friction: \(\sin\phi = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{\sigma_1 + \sigma_3}\) (for sand, \(c = 0\))
  • Failure Plane Angle: \(\theta_f = 45^\circ + \phi/2\) with the major principal plane

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify Principal Stresses: Since \(\sigma_h > \sigma_v\), \(\sigma_1 = 300\text{ kN/m}^2\) and \(\sigma_3 = 100\text{ kN/m}^2\).
    The major principal plane (where \(\sigma_1\) acts) is the vertical plane.
  2. Calculate Angle of Internal Friction (\(\phi\)):
    \[\sin\phi = \dfrac{300 - 100}{300 + 100} = \dfrac{200}{400} = 0.5 \implies \phi = 30^\circ \]
  3. Determine Shearing Plane Angle:
    Failure plane makes an angle \(\theta = 45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi}{2}\) with the major principal plane (vertical):
    \[\theta = 45^\circ + \dfrac{30^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ \text{ (with respect to vertical)} \]
    Therefore, angle with respect to the horizontal:
    \[90^\circ - 60^\circ = 30^\circ \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 30° | Accepted key range: [30 to 30]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q56
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A storm with a recorded precipitation of 11.0 cm, as shown in the table, produced a direct run-off of 6.0 cm.

Time from start (hours)12345678
Recorded cumulative precipitation (cm)0.51.53.15.57.38.910.211.0

The \( \phi \)-index of this storm is _________ cm/hr (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation and Runoff

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Total precipitation = 11.0 cm
    Direct runoff = 6.0 cm
    Cumulative rainfall table over 8 hours
  • Aim: Calculate the \(\phi\)-index.

Core Concepts:

\(\phi\)-index: The average rainfall intensity above which the volume of rainfall equals the volume of runoff. It is an iterative calculation — any hours with rainfall intensity less than the assumed \(\phi\)-index do not contribute to runoff and must be excluded from the effective time calculation.

Solution Method:

Convert cumulative rainfall into hourly increments. Calculate initial average infiltration (W-index). Use this as a first trial for \(\phi\). Exclude hours where rainfall < trial \(\phi\), recalculate, and verify.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Extract Hourly Precipitation (\(P_i\) in cm/hr):
    • Hour 1: 0.5 cm
    • Hour 2: 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 cm
    • Hour 3: 3.1 − 1.5 = 1.6 cm
    • Hour 4: 5.5 − 3.1 = 2.4 cm
    • Hour 5: 7.3 − 5.5 = 1.8 cm
    • Hour 6: 8.9 − 7.3 = 1.6 cm
    • Hour 7: 10.2 − 8.9 = 1.3 cm
    • Hour 8: 11.0 − 10.2 = 0.8 cm
  2. Trial 1 — W-index approximation:
    \[W_{index} = \dfrac{11.0 - 6.0}{8} = 0.625\text{ cm/hr} \]
    Check: Hour 1 rainfall (0.5 cm) < 0.625 cm/hr → produces no runoff and must be excluded.
  3. Trial 2 — Refined \(\phi\):
    Effective Time \(t_e = 8 - 1 = 7\) hours
    Effective Precipitation \(P_e = 11.0 - 0.5 = 10.5\) cm
    \[\phi = \dfrac{P_e - \text{Runoff}}{t_e} = \dfrac{10.5 - 6.0}{7} = \dfrac{4.5}{7} \approx 0.6428\text{ cm/hr} \]
  4. Final Verification: All remaining 7 hours have rainfall ≥ 0.6428 cm/hr (minimum is hour 8 at 0.8 cm/hr). The assumption holds. ✓

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\phi = 0.64\text{ cm/hr}\) | Accepted key range: [0.64 to 0.65]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q57
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 500 m long water distribution pipeline P with diameter 1.0 m, is used to convey 0.1 m³/s of flow. A new pipeline Q, with the same length and flow rate, is to replace P. The friction factors for P and Q are 0.04 and 0.01, respectively. The diameter of the pipeline Q (in meters) is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Pipe Flow

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Pipeline P: \(L = 500\text{ m}\), \(D_P = 1.0\text{ m}\), \(Q = 0.1\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(f_P = 0.04\)
    Pipeline Q: Same \(L\) and \(Q\), \(f_Q = 0.01\)
  • Aim: Find the required diameter of pipeline Q (\(D_Q\)) to functionally replace P.

Core Concepts:

Hydraulic Equivalence: When a pipe replaces another carrying the same flow, it must induce the exact same head loss so the system hydraulics remain balanced.

Darcy-Weisbach Equation: \(h_f = \dfrac{fLQ^2}{12.1\,D^5}\)

Solution Method:

Equate the head loss equations for both pipes. Since \(L\) and \(Q\) are constant, they cancel out, leaving a direct relationship between friction factors and diameters.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Equate Head Losses:
    \[h_{f,P} = h_{f,Q} \implies \dfrac{f_P L Q^2}{12.1\,D_P^5} = \dfrac{f_Q L Q^2}{12.1\,D_Q^5} \]
  2. Simplify and Solve:
    \[\dfrac{f_P}{D_P^5} = \dfrac{f_Q}{D_Q^5} \implies \dfrac{0.04}{1.0^5} = \dfrac{0.01}{D_Q^5} \]\[D_Q^5 = \dfrac{0.01}{0.04} = 0.25 \]\[D_Q = (0.25)^{1/5} \approx 0.7578\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(D_Q \approx 0.76\text{ m}\) | Accepted key range: [0.70 to 0.80]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q58
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A 2 m × 1.5 m tank of 6 m height is provided with a 100 mm diameter orifice at the center of its base. The orifice is plugged and the tank is filled up to 5 m height. Consider the average value of discharge coefficient as 0.6 and acceleration due to gravity (\( g \)) as 10 m/s². After unplugging the orifice, the time (in seconds) taken for the water level to drop from 5 m to 3.5 m under free discharge condition is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Orifice Discharge

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Tank area (\(A\)) \(= 2 \times 1.5 = 3.0\text{ m}^2\)
    Orifice diameter (\(d\)) = 100 mm = 0.1 m
    Initial head (\(h_1\)) = 5 m
    Final head (\(h_2\)) = 3.5 m
    Discharge coefficient (\(C_d\)) = 0.6
    Gravity (\(g\)) = 10 m/s²
  • Aim: Calculate the time taken for the water level to drop from \(h_1\) to \(h_2\).

Core Concepts:

Tank Emptying Equation: Derived by equating the volumetric drop in the tank to the volumetric flow rate through the orifice over time \(dt\):

\[t = \dfrac{2A}{C_d \cdot a \cdot \sqrt{2g}} \left(\sqrt{h_1} - \sqrt{h_2}\right) \]

Solution Method:

Calculate the cross-sectional area of the orifice, then apply the standard tank emptying integral formula directly. Ensure unit consistency (orifice diameter in meters).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Orifice Area (\(a\)):
    \[a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.1)^2 = 0.007854\text{ m}^2 \]
  2. Apply the Emptying Formula:
    \[t = \dfrac{2 \times 3.0}{0.6 \times 0.007854 \times \sqrt{2 \times 10}} \left(\sqrt{5} - \sqrt{3.5}\right) \]\[t = \dfrac{6.0}{0.0047124 \times 4.4721} \times (2.2360 - 1.8708) \]\[t = \dfrac{6.0}{0.021074} \times 0.3652 \]\[t = 284.71 \times 0.3652 \approx 103.98\text{ seconds} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 103.98 seconds | Accepted key range: [102.00 to 106.00]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question: A rectangular channel is 4.0 m wide and carries a discharge of 2.0 m³/s with a depth of 0.4 m. The channel transitions to a maximum width contraction at a downstream location, without influencing the upstream flow conditions. The width (in meters) at the maximum contraction is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Fluid Mechanics | Open Channel Flow (Specific Energy)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Rectangular channel, initial width (\(B_1\)) = 4.0 m
    Discharge (\(Q\)) = 2.0 m³/s
    Initial depth (\(y_1\)) = 0.4 m
    Transition to maximum width contraction without altering upstream flow.
  • Aim: Find the width at the maximum contraction (\(B_2\)).

Core Concepts:

  • Specific Energy (\(E\)): Energy per unit weight of water relative to the channel bottom: \(E = y + \dfrac{V^2}{2g}\)
  • Choking Condition: For maximum contraction without upstream influence, the specific energy at the contracted section (\(E_2\)) must equal the upstream specific energy (\(E_1\)), and flow at the contraction must just reach the critical state.
  • Critical Flow Relations (Rectangular Channel): \(E_c = 1.5\,y_c\)   and   \(y_c = \left(\dfrac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}\), where \(q = Q/B_2\)

Solution Method:

Calculate the specific energy at section 1. Equate to the minimum specific energy required for critical flow at section 2. Back-calculate the critical depth (\(y_c\)), the unit discharge (\(q_2\)), and finally the contracted width (\(B_2\)).

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Upstream Velocity (\(V_1\)):
    \[V_1 = \dfrac{Q}{B_1 \cdot y_1} = \dfrac{2.0}{4.0 \times 0.4} = 1.25\text{ m/s} \]
  2. Calculate Upstream Specific Energy (\(E_1\)):
    \[E_1 = y_1 + \dfrac{V_1^2}{2g} = 0.4 + \dfrac{1.25^2}{2 \times 9.81} = 0.4 + 0.0796 = 0.4796\text{ m} \]
  3. Apply Choking Condition (\(E_1 = E_c\)):
    \[E_c = 1.5\,y_c \implies 0.4796 = 1.5\,y_c \implies y_c = 0.3197\text{ m} \]
  4. Determine Maximum Unit Discharge (\(q_2\)):
    \[y_c^3 = \dfrac{q_2^2}{g} \implies q_2 = \sqrt{g \cdot y_c^3} = \sqrt{9.81 \times (0.3197)^3} = \sqrt{0.3206} = 0.5662\text{ m}^3\text{/s/m} \]
  5. Calculate Contracted Width (\(B_2\)):
    \[B_2 = \dfrac{Q}{q_2} = \dfrac{2.0}{0.5662} = 3.532\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.53 m | Accepted key range: [3.45 to 3.65]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A circular settling tank is to be designed for primary treatment of sewage at a flow rate of 10 million liters/day. Assume a detention period of 2.0 hours and surface loading rate of 40000 liters/m²/day. The height (in meters) of the water column in the tank is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Treatment

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension & Application
  • Given Data:
    Flow rate (\(Q\)) = 10 million liters/day (10 MLD)
    Detention period (\(t_d\)) = 2.0 hours
    Surface loading rate (\(SLR\)) = 40,000 L/m²/day
  • Aim: Calculate the height (\(H\)) of the water column in the primary settling tank.

Core Concepts:

  • Tank Volume (\(V\)): \(V = Q \times t_d\)
  • Surface Area (\(A\)): \(A = \dfrac{Q}{SLR}\)
  • Tank Height: \(H = \dfrac{V}{A} = t_d \times SLR\)

Solution Method:

The height can be obtained by algebraic simplification: \(H = \dfrac{Q \times t_d}{Q / SLR} = t_d \times SLR\). Rigorous unit discipline (hours to days, litres to m³) is essential.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Convert units to compatible systems:
    \(t_d = 2.0\text{ hours} = \dfrac{2}{24}\text{ days} = 0.08333\text{ days}\)
    \(SLR = 40{,}000\text{ L/m}^2\text{/day} = 40\text{ m}^3\text{/m}^2\text{/day}\)
  2. Apply derived formula:
    \[H = t_d \times SLR = 0.08333 \times 40 = 3.333\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 3.33 m | Accepted key range: [3.30 to 3.40]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
An organic waste is represented as C₂₄₀O₂₀₀H₁₈₀N₅S.

(Atomic weights: S-32, H-1, C-12, O-16, N-14).

Assume complete conversion of S to SO₂ while burning.

SO₂ generated (in grams) per kg of this waste is _________ (rounded off to 1 decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Solid Waste Management

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Chemical formula of waste: \(\mathrm{C_{240}O_{200}H_{180}N_5S}\)
    Atomic weights: S = 32, H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, N = 14
    100% conversion of Sulfur to Sulfur Dioxide (\(\mathrm{SO_2}\))
  • Aim: Calculate mass of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) generated (in grams) per 1 kg of waste.

Core Concepts:

Stoichiometry & Molar Mass: One mole of the given waste molecule contains exactly 1 mole of Sulfur atoms, which will oxidize to produce exactly 1 mole of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) molecules.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Molar Mass of Waste (\(MW_{waste}\)):
    \[MW_{waste} = (240 \times 12) + (200 \times 16) + (180 \times 1) + (5 \times 14) + (1 \times 32) \]\[= 2880 + 3200 + 180 + 70 + 32 = 6362\text{ g/mol} \]
  2. Calculate Molar Mass of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\):
    \[MW_{SO_2} = 32 + (2 \times 16) = 64\text{ g/mol} \]
  3. Stoichiometric Ratio: 6362 g of waste produces 64 g of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).
  4. Calculate for 1 kg (1000 g) of waste:
    \[\text{Mass of }\mathrm{SO_2} = \dfrac{64}{6362} \times 1000 = 10.06\text{ g} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 10.1 g | Accepted key range: [10.0 to 10.2]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q62
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
A horizontal curve of radius 1080 m (with transition curves on either side) in a Broad Gauge railway track is designed and constructed for an equilibrium speed of 70 kmph. However, a few years after construction, the Railway Authorities decided to run express trains on this track. The maximum allowable cant deficiency is 10 cm.

The maximum restricted speed (in kmph) of the express trains running on this track is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Railway Track Design

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    Radius (\(R\)) = 1080 m
    Broad Gauge (BG) — Nominal Gauge \(G = 1.676\text{ m}\)
    Equilibrium speed (\(V_{eq}\)) = 70 kmph
    Max cant deficiency (\(C_d\)) = 10 cm = 0.1 m
  • Aim: Find maximum restricted speed (\(V_{max}\)) in kmph for express trains.

Core Concepts:

  • Equilibrium Cant (\(e_{eq}\)): \(e_{eq} = \dfrac{G \cdot V_{eq}^2}{127R}\)
  • Cant Deficiency (\(C_d\)): Express trains run faster than equilibrium speed, requiring more cant than provided. The shortfall is cant deficiency.
  • Maximum Allowable Cant: \(e_{max} = e_{eq} + C_d\)
  • Maximum Speed: \(V_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{e_{max} \cdot 127 \cdot R}{G}}\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Equilibrium Cant (\(e_{eq}\)):
    \[e_{eq} = \dfrac{1.676 \times 70^2}{127 \times 1080} = \dfrac{1.676 \times 4900}{137160} = 0.05986\text{ m} = 5.986\text{ cm} \]
  2. Calculate Maximum Theoretical Cant (\(e_{max}\)):
    \[e_{max} = e_{eq} + C_d = 5.986 + 10.0 = 15.986\text{ cm} = 0.15986\text{ m} \]
  3. Calculate Maximum Restricted Speed (\(V_{max}\)):
    \[V_{max}^2 = \dfrac{e_{max} \times 127 \times R}{G} = \dfrac{0.15986 \times 127 \times 1080}{1.676} = 13083 \]\[V_{max} = \sqrt{13083} = 114.38\text{ kmph} \]

Note: Using dynamic gauge of 1.75 m yields ~113 kmph. Both 113 and 114 are typically accepted in GATE keys.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 114 kmph | Accepted key range: [112 to 115]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q63
questions.subject: Transportation Engineering
questions.question:
A vertical summit curve on a freight corridor is formed at the intersection of two gradients, +3.0% and −5.0%.

Assume the following:
Only large-sized trucks are allowed on this corridor
Design speed = 80 kmph
Eye height of truck drivers above the road surface = 2.30 m
Height of object above the road surface for which trucks need to stop = 0.35 m
Total reaction time of the truck drivers = 2.0 s
Coefficient of longitudinal friction of the road = 0.36
Stopping sight distance gets compensated on the gradient

The design length of the summit curve (in meters) to accommodate the stopping sight distance is _________ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Transportation Engineering | Geometric Design of Highways

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Gradients: \(N_1 = +0.03\), \(N_2 = -0.05\)
    Design speed (\(v\)) = 80 kmph = 22.22 m/s
    Eye height (\(H\)) = 2.30 m; Object height (\(h\)) = 0.35 m
    Reaction time (\(t\)) = 2.0 s; Friction (\(f\)) = 0.36
    Constraint: "Stopping sight distance gets compensated on the gradient."
  • Aim: Design length of summit curve (\(L\)).

Core Concepts:

  • Deviation Angle: \(N = N_1 - N_2\)
  • Stopping Sight Distance (SSD): \(SSD = v \cdot t + \dfrac{v^2}{2gf}\)
    The phrase "compensated on the gradient" implies the gradient effect is negated — SSD is computed as if on a level grade.
  • Curve Length Formulas:
    For \(L > SSD\): \(L = \dfrac{N \cdot S^2}{2(\sqrt{H} + \sqrt{h})^2}\)
    For \(L < SSD\): \(L = 2S - \dfrac{2(\sqrt{H} + \sqrt{h})^2}{N}\)

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Level SSD (\(S\)):
    \[S = (22.22 \times 2.0) + \dfrac{22.22^2}{2 \times 9.81 \times 0.36} = 44.444 + \dfrac{493.728}{7.0632} = 44.444 + 69.901 = 114.345\text{ m} \]
  2. Calculate Deviation Angle (\(N\)):
    \[N = 0.03 - (-0.05) = 0.08 \]
  3. Assume \(L > S\) and Calculate \(L\):
    \[L = \dfrac{0.08 \times (114.345)^2}{2(\sqrt{2.30} + \sqrt{0.35})^2} \]\[\text{Denominator} = 2(1.5166 + 0.5916)^2 = 2(2.1082)^2 = 2 \times 4.444 = 8.889 \]\[L = \dfrac{0.08 \times 13074.8}{8.889} = \dfrac{1045.98}{8.889} = 117.67\text{ m} \]
  4. Validation: 117.67 m > 114.345 m → Assumption (\(L > S\)) holds. ✓

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 117.67 m | Accepted key range: [117.00 to 118.50]

questions.title: GATE CE 2024 Set 2 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Surveying & Geomatics
questions.question: A child walks on a level surface from point P to point Q at a bearing of 30°, from point Q to point R at a bearing of 90° and then directly returns to the starting point P at a bearing of 240°. The straight-line paths PQ and QR are 4 m each. Assuming that all bearings are measured from the magnetic north in degrees, the straight-line path length RP (in meters) is _________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Traversing & Bearings

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    P to Q: Bearing \(\theta_{PQ} = 30^\circ\), Length = 4 m
    Q to R: Bearing \(\theta_{QR} = 90^\circ\), Length = 4 m
    R to P: Bearing \(\theta_{RP} = 240^\circ\)
  • Aim: Find straight-line path length RP.

Core Concepts:

Latitudes and Departures: Coordinates in surveying are defined relative to the North (\(+Y\) axis).

  • Latitude: \(\Delta Y = L\cos\theta\)
  • Departure: \(\Delta X = L\sin\theta\)

Solution Method:

Set P as the origin (0, 0). Calculate coordinates of Q, then R. Use the distance formula between P and R. The given back bearing of \(240^\circ\) serves as a consistency check.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Coordinates of Q:
    \[X_Q = 0 + 4\sin(30^\circ) = 4 \times 0.5 = 2.0\text{ m} \]\[Y_Q = 0 + 4\cos(30^\circ) = 4 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3.464\text{ m} \]
  2. Coordinates of R:
    \[X_R = 2.0 + 4\sin(90^\circ) = 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0\text{ m} \]\[Y_R = 3.464 + 4\cos(90^\circ) = 3.464 + 0 = 3.464\text{ m} \]
  3. Calculate Distance RP:
    \[RP = \sqrt{(6.0)^2 + (3.464)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 12} = \sqrt{48} = 6.928\text{ m} \]
  4. Validation via Back Bearing:
    Bearing of R from P: \(\tan^{-1}(6.0/3.464) = 60^\circ\). Back-bearing from R to P: \(60^\circ + 180^\circ = 240^\circ\). ✓ Matches given data.
  5. Rounding to nearest integer: \(6.928 \rightarrow 7\)

Final Answer:

questions.question:
Differential levelling is carried out from point P (BM: +200.000 m) to point R. The readings taken are given in the table.

PointsStaff readings (m)Remarks
Back SightFore Sight
P(−)2.050BM: +200.000 m
Q1.0500.950Q is a change point
R(−)1.655

Reduced Level (in meters) of the point R is _________ (rounded off to 3 decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Geomatics Engineering | Differential Levelling

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Bench Mark (P): RL = +200.000 m, BS = (−)2.050 m
    Point Q (Change point): BS = 1.050 m, FS = 0.950 m
    Point R: FS = (−)1.655 m
  • Aim: Calculate the Reduced Level (RL) of point R.

Core Concepts:

Height of Instrument (HI) Method:

  • \(HI = RL + BS\)
  • \(RL_{new} = HI - FS\)

Inverted Staff Readings: Indicated by negative signs — the point being measured is physically above the instrument's line of sight (e.g., soffit of a bridge or roof). The negative sign must be maintained in the algebraic sum.

Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. First Instrument Setup:
    \[HI_1 = RL_P + BS_P = 200.000 + (-2.050) = 197.950\text{ m} \]\[RL_Q = HI_1 - FS_Q = 197.950 - 0.950 = 197.000\text{ m} \]
  2. Second Instrument Setup (after change point Q):
    \[HI_2 = RL_Q + BS_Q = 197.000 + 1.050 = 198.050\text{ m} \]\[RL_R = HI_2 - FS_R = 198.050 - (-1.655) = 198.050 + 1.655 = 199.705\text{ m} \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 199.705 m | Accepted key range: [199.705 to 199.705]
